source.text: לֹא־יִקַּ֥ח אִ֖ישׁ אֶת־אֵ֣שֶׁת אָבִ֑יו וְלֹ֥א יְגַלֶּ֖ה כְּנַ֥ף אָבִֽיו׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Not shall take a man [the] wife of his father, and not he shall uncover [the] skirt of his father.

en.L: A man shall not take his father's wife, and he shall not uncover his father's skirt.
en.B: A man must not marry his father's wife; he must not uncover the edge of his father's garment.
en.R: A man must not marry his father's wife. He must not take for himself the woman who belongs to his father.

decisions.choice: verse numbers: in many Bibles this verse is 22:30
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. In the Hebrew text this verse opens chapter 23; many Bibles number it 22:30, the last verse of chapter 22, and so number the rest of this chapter (23:2-26 here) 23:1-25. The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: take his father's wife: marry her, or take her as his own, after the father's death or divorce
decisions.reason: "Take" a woman is the usual way of saying "marry" (22:13-14; 24:1). The father's wife here is a wife other than the man's own mother: a stepmother, or a widow of the father. Leviticus 18:8 and 20:11 forbid the same union, and 27:20 below puts a curse on it. Reuben's act with his father's concubine shows how seriously it was taken (Genesis 35:22; 49:4).

decisions.choice: uncover his father's skirt: violate what belongs to his father in marriage
alternatives: a separate act of indecency toward the father himself
decisions.reason: To spread the edge of one's garment over a woman was a sign of taking her as wife (Ruth 3:9; Ezekiel 16:8). To uncover the father's garment is to lay bare what that covering protects, his marriage, and so to shame him. The same words return in 27:20.

decisions.choice: still Moses speaking: part of the speech that began at 5:1
decisions.reason: The chapter lies inside Moses' long speech of 5:1-26:19, so no new speech begins here. This verse rounds off the laws on marriage and sexual wrongs in 22:13-29.

decisions.choice: the edge of his father's garment
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word means a wing or the corner of a garment. Balanced keeps the picture and says "edge of ... garment" so it is not read as a modern skirt; Literal keeps "skirt".

decisions.choice: take for himself the woman who belongs to his father
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means (m3) instead of keeping it.

source.text: לֹֽא־יָבֹ֧א פְצֽוּעַ־דַּכָּ֛א וּכְר֥וּת שָׁפְכָ֖ה בִּקְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Not shall enter [one] wounded of crushing and [one] cut off of [the] male organ into [the] assembly of Yahweh.

en.L: One wounded by crushing or cut off in the male organ shall not enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: No man whose testicles have been crushed or whose penis has been cut off may enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: A man whose sex organs have been crushed or cut off may not join the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: verse numbers: many Bibles begin chapter 23 here
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. Many Bibles count the verse before this one as 22:30 and begin chapter 23 here, so 23:2-26 here is 23:1-25 there. The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: wounded by crushing ... cut off: a man whose testicles have been crushed or whose penis has been cut off
decisions.reason: The first phrase names injury by crushing, most likely of the testicles (Leviticus 21:20; 22:24 use related words for blemished priests and animals); the second names cutting off of the male organ. Both describe men made unable to father children, whether by injury or, as was done to some royal servants and to devotees of certain gods, on purpose.

decisions.choice: enter the assembly of the LORD: belong to the people of Israel when they gather before the LORD
decisions.reason: "The assembly of the LORD" is Israel gathered as God's people, for worship, covenant and decision (4:10; 9:10; 31:30). To "enter" it is to be counted as a full member of it. The verse does not forbid such a man to live among Israel; the rules in verses 2-9 concern who may be counted in the assembly.

decisions.choice: later promise to eunuchs
decisions.reason: Isaiah 56:3-5 later promises eunuchs who keep the covenant a name and a place in God's house better than sons and daughters, looking beyond this rule.

decisions.choice: testicles ... penis / sex organs
decisions.reason: Balanced names the body parts plainly, as the Hebrew does; Readable uses a general phrase that is suitable for young readers. Literal keeps "crushing" and "the male organ".

source.text: לֹא־יָבֹ֥א מַמְזֵ֖ר בִּקְהַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה גַּ֚ם דּ֣וֹר עֲשִׂירִ֔י לֹא־יָ֥בֹא ל֖וֹ בִּקְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Not shall enter [one of] forbidden birth into [the] assembly of Yahweh; also a generation tenth, not shall enter of his into [the] assembly of Yahweh.

en.L: One of forbidden birth shall not enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; even the tenth generation, none of his shall enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. None of their descendants may enter it, not even in the tenth generation.
en.R: No one born from a forbidden marriage may join the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Even ten generations later, none of that person's descendants may join it.

decisions.choice: one of forbidden birth: a child of a union the law forbids
alternatives: a child of a marriage with a foreigner
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is rare (here and Zechariah 9:6) and its meaning is not certain. Coming right after verse 1, it most likely names a child born of a union forbidden by the law, such as incest (Leviticus 18:6-18). In Zechariah 9:6 it names a mixed or alien people settling in a Philistine town, so some take it here as a child of a marriage between an Israelite and a foreigner. It does not mean simply a child born to unmarried parents.

decisions.choice: even the tenth generation: never
decisions.reason: Ten generations stands for a full and final span of time. In verse 4 the same phrase is followed by "forever", which shows that it means a lasting ban, not one that ends after ten generations (Nehemiah 13:1).

decisions.choice: their descendants
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "of his", meaning the person's offspring. Balanced says "their" because the rule covers anyone of such birth, male or female; Readable says "that person's". Literal keeps "of his".

source.text: לֹֽא־יָבֹ֧א עַמּוֹנִ֛י וּמוֹאָבִ֖י בִּקְהַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה גַּ֚ם דּ֣וֹר עֲשִׂירִ֔י לֹא־יָבֹ֥א לָהֶ֛ם בִּקְהַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה עַד־עוֹלָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Not shall enter [an] Ammonite and [a] Moabite into [the] assembly of Yahweh; also a generation tenth, not shall enter of them into [the] assembly of Yahweh until perpetuity,

en.L: An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; even the tenth generation, none of them shall enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} forever,
en.B: No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. None of them may ever enter it, not even in the tenth generation,
en.R: No Ammonite or Moabite may join the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Even ten generations later, none of their people may ever join it.

decisions.choice: Ammonite and Moabite: the peoples east of the Jordan descended from Lot
decisions.reason: Genesis 19:30-38 traces Moab and Ammon to Lot's two daughters. Israel was told not to attack them on the way to the land (2:9, 19). Their exclusion from the assembly rests on what they did when Israel passed by, given in verse 5.

decisions.choice: even the tenth generation ... forever: the ban never ends
decisions.reason: As in verse 3, "the tenth generation" stands for a full span, and here "forever" is added. Nehemiah 13:1-3 quotes this verse when the people separate from those of foreign descent.

decisions.choice: Ruth the Moabite: a later story that sits beside this law
alternatives: the law applies to men only
the law applies to all of both peoples
decisions.reason: Ruth, a woman of Moab, joins Israel, marries Boaz and becomes the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 1:16; 4:13-22). The book does not explain how that fits with this verse. Later Jewish teaching took the masculine forms here to apply to men only; the verse itself does not say.

decisions.choice: None of them may ever enter it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable move "forever" into the main clause so the point is clear: the ban has no end. The sentence goes on into verse 5, which gives the reason; Readable ends here and starts verse 5 with "This is because".

source.text: עַל־דְּבַ֞ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹא־קִדְּמ֤וּ אֶתְכֶם֙ בַּלֶּ֣חֶם וּבַמַּ֔יִם בַּדֶּ֖רֶךְ בְּצֵאתְכֶ֣ם מִמִּצְרָ֑יִם וַאֲשֶׁר֩ שָׂכַ֨ר עָלֶ֜יךָ אֶת־בִּלְעָ֣ם בֶּן־בְּע֗וֹר מִפְּת֛וֹר אֲרַ֥ם נַהֲרַ֖יִם לְקַֽלְלֶֽךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: because of [the] matter that not they met you with bread and with water on the way in your going out from Egypt, and that he hired against you Balaam son of Beor from Pethor of Aram-naharaim to curse you.

en.L: because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because he hired against you Balaam son of Beor from Pethor of Aram-naharaim to curse you.
en.B: because they did not come to meet you with food and water on your journey after you left Egypt, and because Moab hired Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor in Aram-naharaim, to put a curse on you.
en.R: This is because they did not come out with food and water to welcome you on your journey after you left Egypt. And the king of Moab paid Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor in Mesopotamia, to put a curse on you.

decisions.choice: meet you with bread and water: greet travelers with food as a welcome
decisions.reason: To go out and meet travelers with bread and water was a basic act of hospitality to people passing through (Genesis 14:18; 1 Samuel 25:18). Moses had asked Edom and Moab to sell food and water (2:6, 28-29); the charge here is that Ammon and Moab offered no welcome to a people in need.

decisions.choice: he hired: the king of Moab
decisions.reason: The subject changes from "they" (both peoples) to "he". It was Balak king of Moab who sent for Balaam (Numbers 22:2-7), so "he" is Moab, or its king. The address also moves from "you" plural to "you" singular, as Deuteronomy often does.

decisions.choice: Balaam son of Beor: the seer Balak hired to curse Israel
decisions.reason: Numbers 22-24 tells the story: Balaam came, but the LORD made him bless Israel instead (Numbers 23:11; 24:10). Verse 6 sums up the outcome.

decisions.choice: Pethor of Aram-naharaim: a town in upper Mesopotamia
decisions.reason: Aram-naharaim means "Aram of the two rivers", the land in the bend of the Euphrates in upper Mesopotamia (Genesis 24:10). Pethor lay near the Euphrates, "the River" (Numbers 22:5).

decisions.choice: Moab / the king of Moab
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he". Balanced names Moab and Readable names its king, to show who "he" is (m2).

decisions.choice: Mesopotamia
decisions.reason: Readable gives the familiar name of the region for Aram-naharaim. Literal and Balanced keep the Hebrew name.

source.text: וְלֹֽא־אָבָ֞ה יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ לִשְׁמֹ֣עַ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַיַּהֲפֹךְ֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֧יךָ לְּךָ֛ אֶת־הַקְּלָלָ֖ה לִבְרָכָ֑ה כִּ֥י אֲהֵֽבְךָ֖ יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And not was willing Yahweh your God to listen to Balaam, and turned Yahweh your God for you the curse into blessing, for loved you Yahweh your God.

en.L: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God was not willing to listen to Balaam, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God loved you.
en.B: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God refused to listen to Balaam. Instead {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God made the curse a blessing for you, since {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God loved you.
en.R: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God would not listen to Balaam. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God loved you, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} changed the curse into a blessing for you.

decisions.choice: not willing to listen ... turned the curse into a blessing
decisions.reason: Each time Balaam set out to curse Israel, the LORD put a blessing in his mouth instead (Numbers 23:7-10, 18-24; 24:3-9). Nehemiah 13:2 repeats this verse. The LORD did not grant Balaam's wish to curse, so his attempt only produced blessing.

decisions.choice: because the LORD your God loved you: the reason is God's own love
alternatives: because the LORD your God loves you
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy grounds Israel's rescue and blessing in God's love, not in Israel's merit (4:37; 7:7-8; 10:15). The verb is in a form that can be read either as "loved" (when Balaam came) or as "loves".

decisions.choice: loved you, so he changed
decisions.reason: Readable puts the reason first and refers to the LORD the third time with a pronoun, to keep the sentence short. Literal and Balanced keep the Hebrew order and the repeated name.

decisions.choice: refused to listen
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "was not willing to listen". Balanced says "refused", which carries the same sense of a firm choice; Literal keeps "was not willing".

source.text: לֹא־תִדְרֹ֥שׁ שְׁלֹמָ֖ם וְטֹבָתָ֑ם כָּל־יָמֶ֖יךָ לְעוֹלָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Not you shall seek their peace and their good all your days forever.

en.L: You shall not seek their peace or their good all your days, forever.
en.B: Never seek a peace treaty with them or work for their prosperity, as long as you live as a people.
en.R: As long as your nation lasts, never make a peace treaty with them or try to help them do well.

decisions.choice: seek their peace and their good: make treaties of friendship with them and promote their welfare
alternatives: never wish them well in any way
decisions.reason: "Peace" and "good" were used for friendly relations between nations, sealed by treaty (1 Kings 5:26; Jeremiah 29:7 uses "seek the peace" of a city). The command forbids Israel as a nation to seek alliance and friendship with Ammon and Moab. It does not order hatred of every person of those peoples, as Ruth shows. Ezra 9:12 quotes it of marriages with neighboring peoples.

decisions.choice: all your days forever: for as long as Israel exists
decisions.reason: The "you" is Israel as one people, so "all your days" is the life of the nation, and "forever" stresses it, as in verse 4.

decisions.choice: a peace treaty ... their prosperity
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "peace" and "good" mean between nations (m1). Literal keeps the bare words.

decisions.choice: as long as you live as a people / as long as your nation lasts
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that "your days" is the life of the people, not of one person (m2).

source.text: לֹֽא־תְתַעֵ֣ב אֲדֹמִ֔י כִּ֥י אָחִ֖יךָ ה֑וּאסלֹא־תְתַעֵ֣ב מִצְרִ֔י כִּי־גֵ֖ר הָיִ֥יתָ בְאַרְצֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Not you shall abhor [an] Edomite, for your brother [is] he; not you shall abhor [an] Egyptian, for [a] sojourner you were in his land.

en.L: You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he [is] your brother; you shall not abhor an Egyptian, for you were a sojourner in his land.
en.B: Do not detest an Edomite, for he is your relative. Do not detest an Egyptian, because you lived as a outsider in his land.
en.R: Do not hate an Edomite, because the Edomites are your relatives. Do not hate an Egyptian, because you once lived as outsiders in their country.

decisions.choice: your brother: Edom descends from Esau, Jacob's brother
decisions.reason: Edom's people came from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob, who is Israel (Genesis 25:24-26; 36:1). Israel was told not to provoke them on the way (2:4-8). "Brother" here means a related people.

decisions.choice: you were a sojourner in his land: Israel lived in Egypt as foreigners
decisions.reason: Jacob's family went down to Egypt and was received there in a time of famine (Genesis 45-47). Though Egypt later made them slaves, Israel is to remember that it first found shelter there. The same reason is given for loving the sojourner (10:19).

decisions.choice: abhor: treat as detestable and shut out
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for "abomination" (17:1; 23:19). Israel is not to treat these two peoples as utterly unacceptable, as it must Ammon and Moab; verse 9 gives the result.

decisions.choice: relative / relatives
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "brother". Balanced and Readable say "relative", since a whole related people is meant (m1).

decisions.choice: you once lived as outsiders
decisions.reason: Readable makes the singular "you" plural, since the whole people lived in Egypt. Literal keeps "sojourner"; Balanced says "outsider", as for the sojourner elsewhere in Deuteronomy.

source.text: בָּנִ֛ים אֲשֶׁר־יִוָּלְד֥וּ לָהֶ֖ם דּ֣וֹר שְׁלִישִׁ֑י יָבֹ֥א לָהֶ֖ם בִּקְהַ֥ל יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Children who will be born to them, [the] generation third, may enter of them into [the] assembly of Yahweh.

en.L: Children who are born to them, the third generation of them, may enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: The children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Their grandchildren, the third generation, may join the assembly of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: the third generation: the grandchildren of those who first come to live in Israel
decisions.reason: "Them" are the Edomites and Egyptians of verse 8 who settle among Israel. Counting the settlers as the first generation, their grandchildren are the third. Some count the settlers' children as the first born "to them", which would make the third generation their great-grandchildren.

decisions.choice: may enter: the way into the assembly is open to them
decisions.reason: Unlike Ammon and Moab (verse 4), Edomites and Egyptians who live among Israel can in time be counted as full members of the LORD's assembly.

decisions.choice: grandchildren
decisions.reason: Readable says who the third generation are, following the counting in m1, and keeps "the third generation" beside it. If the other way of counting is right, the word would be "great-grandchildren". Literal and Balanced keep only "third generation".

source.text: כִּֽי־תֵצֵ֥א מַחֲנֶ֖ה עַל־אֹיְבֶ֑יךָ וְנִ֨שְׁמַרְתָּ֔ מִכֹּ֖ל דָּבָ֥ר רָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: When you go out [as a] camp against your enemies, and you shall keep yourself from every thing evil.

en.L: When you go out [as] a camp against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing.
en.B: When you go out and camp against your enemies, guard yourself against anything that is wrong.
en.R: When your army goes out and sets up camp to fight your enemies, stay away from everything that is wrong.

decisions.choice: go out as a camp: set out on campaign and camp as an army
decisions.reason: "Camp" stands without a preposition, describing how Israel goes out: as an army encamped. The rules that follow (verses 11-15) are for the war camp, where the LORD himself is present (verse 15).

decisions.choice: every evil thing: anything improper, including what makes a person or the camp unclean
decisions.reason: "Thing" can also mean "word" or "matter", and "evil" covers what is bad of any kind. The verses that follow show that it includes bodily uncleanness and filth, not only moral wrongs. The same "thing" returns in verse 15 ("anything indecent").

decisions.choice: your army goes out and sets up camp to fight
decisions.reason: Readable names the army and says what "go out as a camp against" means (m1). Literal and Balanced keep the shorter wording.

source.text: כִּֽי־יִהְיֶ֤ה בְךָ֙ אִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹא־יִהְיֶ֥ה טָה֖וֹר מִקְּרֵה־לָ֑יְלָה וְיָצָא֙ אֶל־מִח֣וּץ לַֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה לֹ֥א יָבֹ֖א אֶל־תּ֥וֹךְ הַֽמַּחֲנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: If there is among you a man who not is clean from [a] happening of [the] night, and he shall go out to outside of the camp; not he shall come into [the] midst of the camp.

en.L: If there is among you a man who is not clean because of something that happened at night, then he shall go out outside the camp; he shall not come into the midst of the camp.
en.B: If any man among you is unclean because of an emission during the night, he must go outside the camp and not come inside it.
en.R: A man may become unclean because he had a discharge of semen in the night. If that happens, he must go outside the camp and stay out of it.

decisions.choice: not clean because of a happening of the night: unclean after a discharge of semen during sleep
decisions.reason: "A happening of the night" is a modest way of naming a seminal emission in sleep. Leviticus 15:16 makes a man unclean until evening after such an emission. In the holy war camp (verse 15) he must stay outside while he is unclean.

decisions.choice: an emission during the night / a discharge of semen in the night
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew's indirect phrase. Balanced and Readable say what it refers to (m1), Readable in plainer words.

decisions.choice: stay out of it
decisions.reason: Readable says "stay out" for "not come into the midst of the camp"; verse 12 says when he may return.

source.text: וְהָיָ֥ה לִפְנֽוֹת־עֶ֖רֶב יִרְחַ֣ץ בַּמָּ֑יִם וּכְבֹ֣א הַשֶּׁ֔מֶשׁ יָבֹ֖א אֶל־תּ֥וֹךְ הַֽמַּחֲנֶה׃

records.literal_gloss: And it shall be, at [the] turning of evening he shall wash with water, and at [the] going of the sun he may come into [the] midst of the camp.

en.L: And it shall be, at the turning of evening he shall wash with water, and when the sun goes down he may come into the midst of the camp.
en.B: Toward evening he is to bathe in water, and at sunset he may come back into the camp.
en.R: Late in the day he must wash himself with water. When the sun has gone down, he may come back into the camp.

decisions.choice: toward evening ... when the sun goes down: the uncleanness lasts until evening
decisions.reason: Leviticus 15:16 says that a man after an emission must bathe in water and is unclean until evening. A new day began at sunset, so after washing he is clean again with the new day and may return.

decisions.choice: bathe in water
decisions.reason: The verb means to wash, often the whole body (Leviticus 15:16). Balanced says "bathe"; Literal and Readable say "wash".

source.text: וְיָד֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה לְךָ֔ מִח֖וּץ לַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה וְיָצָ֥אתָ שָׁ֖מָּה חֽוּץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [a] hand shall be for you outside of the camp, and you shall go out there outside.

en.L: And you shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there, outside.
en.B: Have a place set aside outside the camp, and go out there when you need to relieve yourself.
en.R: Choose a spot outside the camp where you can go to the toilet. Go out there to do it.

decisions.choice: hand: a marked place, a set area
decisions.reason: The word means "hand", but it can mean a place or a marker that sets a place apart (Numbers 2:17, "each in his place"; 1 Samuel 15:12, a monument). Here it is a set area outside the camp, and verse 14 shows what it is for.

decisions.choice: go out there: to relieve oneself
decisions.reason: Verse 14 makes clear that the place is a latrine. Waste was to be kept outside the camp.

decisions.choice: place / spot
decisions.reason: Every level says what the word means here (m1), since "hand" would not be understood. Literal says "place".

decisions.choice: when you need to relieve yourself / to do it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state now the purpose that verse 14 shows (m2). Readable says "go to the toilet", the everyday phrase for it.

source.text: וְיָתֵ֛ד תִּהְיֶ֥ה לְךָ֖ עַל־אֲזֵנֶ֑ךָ וְהָיָה֙ בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ֣ ח֔וּץ וְחָפַרְתָּ֣ה בָ֔הּ וְשַׁבְתָּ֖ וְכִסִּ֥יתָ אֶת־צֵאָתֶֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [a] spade shall be for you with your equipment, and it shall be, when you sit outside, and you shall dig with it and turn and cover your excrement.

en.L: And you shall have a peg with your equipment, and it shall be, when you sit down outside, you shall dig with it, and turn and cover your excrement.
en.B: Carry a digging tool among your gear, and when you squat outside, dig a hole with it, and then cover up your excrement.
en.R: Keep a digging stick with your gear. When you go outside to relieve yourself, dig a hole with it. Then cover up your waste.

decisions.choice: peg: a pointed stake used as a digging tool
decisions.reason: The word is the name for a tent peg (Judges 4:21; Exodus 27:19). Here it is a pointed stick or small spade carried for digging.

decisions.choice: equipment: the soldier's gear, perhaps his weapons
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here, and its exact sense is not known. It is related to words for tools, and may mean weapons or kit. Either way the digging tool is part of what each man carries.

decisions.choice: when you sit outside: when you relieve yourself
decisions.reason: "Sit" here is a modest way of speaking of relieving oneself. "Turn" after "dig" means to go back and do the next thing: cover the waste.

decisions.choice: digging tool / digging stick
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "peg". Balanced and Readable name its use (m1).

decisions.choice: squat / go outside to relieve yourself; then
decisions.reason: Balanced says "squat" for "sit"; Readable says what is meant. Both render "turn" as "then", as m3 explains. Literal keeps "sit" and "turn".

source.text: כִּי֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ מִתְהַלֵּ֣ךְ׀בְּקֶ֣רֶב מַחֲנֶ֗ךָ לְהַצִּֽילְךָ֙ וְלָתֵ֤ת אֹיְבֶ֨יךָ֙ לְפָנֶ֔יךָ וְהָיָ֥ה מַחֲנֶ֖יךָ קָד֑וֹשׁ וְלֹֽא־יִרְאֶ֤ה בְךָ֙ עֶרְוַ֣ת דָּבָ֔ר וְשָׁ֖ב מֵאַחֲרֶֽיךָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For Yahweh your God [is] walking about in [the] midst of your camp to deliver you and to give your enemies before you, and shall be your camps holy, and not he shall see among you nakedness of a thing and turn back from after you.

en.L: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God walks about in the midst of your camp to deliver you and to give your enemies before you, and your camp shall be holy, so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} does not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.
en.B: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God moves about in your camp to rescue you and to hand your enemies over to you. So your camp must be holy, or {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may see something indecent among you and turn away from you.
en.R: This is because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God walks around in your camp. He is there to keep you safe and to give you victory over your enemies. So your camp must be holy. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will not see anything shameful among you and turn away from you.

decisions.choice: walks about in the midst of your camp: the LORD is present with Israel's army
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of God walking in the garden (Genesis 3:8) and of his promise to walk among his people (Leviticus 26:12). In war the LORD goes with Israel and fights for them (20:4). Because he is present, the camp must be fit for him.

decisions.choice: to give your enemies before you: to give you victory over them
decisions.reason: "Give ... before you" means to hand over to Israel in defeat (7:2, 23; 31:5).

decisions.choice: nakedness of a thing: something indecent or shameful
decisions.reason: The phrase joins "nakedness" with "thing" and names something exposed that ought to be covered, here filth left in the open. The same phrase in 24:1 is the ground for a divorce.

decisions.choice: your camps: the camp in each place it is set up
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "camps" in the plural, either the camp each time the army sets up, or the several camps of one army. The verse began with "your camp" in the singular; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: hand your enemies over to you / give you victory over your enemies
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means (m2). Literal keeps "give your enemies before you".

decisions.choice: your camp
decisions.reason: Every level says "camp" in the singular for the plural "camps" (m4), since it is the same camp as at the start of the verse.

source.text: לֹא־תַסְגִּ֥יר עֶ֖בֶד אֶל־אֲדֹנָ֑יו אֲשֶׁר־יִנָּצֵ֥ל אֵלֶ֖יךָ מֵעִ֥ם אֲדֹנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Not you shall hand over [a] slave to his master who escapes to you from with his master.

en.L: You shall not hand over to his master a slave who escapes to you from his master.
en.B: If a slave has escaped from his master and taken refuge with you, do not hand him back to his master.
en.R: If a slave runs away from his master and comes to you for safety, do not send him back to his master.

decisions.choice: a slave who escapes to you: most likely a slave fleeing from a foreign land
alternatives: a slave fleeing an Israelite master
decisions.reason: "To you" is Israel as a people, and verse 17 lets the slave settle in any of Israel's towns. So the case is most likely a slave who has fled from abroad into Israel. Treaties between kings in the ancient world often required runaway slaves to be sent back; this law forbids it. Whether it also covers a slave fleeing an Israelite master the text does not say.

decisions.choice: slave: a person owned by a master
decisions.reason: The word names someone in the service of a master and here owned by him, since he has a master to flee from.

decisions.choice: his master: a plural form used for one master
decisions.reason: The word for "master" is plural in form, as it often is when one owner is meant (Genesis 39:20; Exodus 21:4). It means one master.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "slave": the law is about a person who is owned and has run away from his owner, so slavery itself is the point and "servant" would weaken it.

decisions.choice: If a slave has escaped ... do not hand him back
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the escape first and the command second, as English tells a case. Literal keeps the Hebrew order.

source.text: עִמְּךָ֞ יֵשֵׁ֣ב בְּקִרְבְּךָ֗ בַּמָּק֧וֹם אֲשֶׁר־יִבְחַ֛ר בְּאַחַ֥ד שְׁעָרֶ֖יךָ בַּטּ֣וֹב ל֑וֹ לֹ֖א תּוֹנֶֽנּוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: With you he shall dwell, in your midst, in the place which he chooses in one of your gates, in the good to him; not you shall oppress him.

en.L: With you he shall dwell, in your midst, in the place that he chooses in one of your gates, where it is good to him; you shall not oppress him.
en.B: Let him live among you, in the place he chooses in any one of your towns, wherever suits him best. Do not mistreat him.
en.R: Let him live with you in whatever town he chooses, wherever he likes best. Do not treat him badly.

decisions.choice: the place which he chooses: the slave's free choice, in the words used for the LORD's chosen place
decisions.reason: "The place which he chooses" is the phrase Deuteronomy uses over and over for the place the LORD will choose for his name (12:5, 11, 14). Here the one who chooses is the runaway slave. The freedom to choose where to live is his own.

decisions.choice: oppress: mistreat or take advantage of
decisions.reason: The verb is used for wronging the weak, above all the sojourner (Exodus 22:20; Leviticus 19:33). The slave who has fled may not be exploited by those who take him in.

decisions.choice: your gates: your towns
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in Deuteronomy, "your gates" stands for the towns of Israel (17:2).

decisions.choice: towns
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "gates". Balanced and Readable say "towns", the thing the word stands for here (m3).

source.text: לֹא־תִהְיֶ֥ה קְדֵשָׁ֖ה מִבְּנ֣וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה קָדֵ֖שׁ מִבְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵל׃

records.literal_gloss: Not shall be [a] female cult prostitute from [the] daughters of Israel, and not shall be [a] male cult prostitute from [the] sons of Israel.

en.L: There shall be no female cult prostitute among the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no male cult prostitute among the sons of Israel.
en.B: No Israelite woman is to become a shrine prostitute, and no Israelite man is to become a shrine prostitute.
en.R: No Israelite woman or man may work as a prostitute at a shrine.

decisions.choice: a woman or man given over to sexual service connected with a shrine
alternatives: a consecrated woman or man serving at a shrine, without sexual service
decisions.reason: The two words come from the root meaning "holy" or "set apart", and name a woman and a man set apart for a god or a shrine. In Genesis 38:15, 21-22 the same woman is called a "prostitute" and a "cult prostitute", and Hosea 4:14 sets the word beside prostitutes at sacrifices, so sexual service is in view. How such service worked, and whether it was a rite of worship or prostitution practiced at shrines, is not certain. Kings of Judah later removed such men from the land (1 Kings 15:12; 2 Kings 23:7).

decisions.choice: of the daughters ... of the sons of Israel: no Israelite woman or man
decisions.reason: "Daughters of Israel" and "sons of Israel" mean Israelite women and Israelite men. The law forbids any of the people to take this role.

decisions.choice: shrine prostitute / prostitute at a shrine
decisions.reason: Literal says "cult prostitute". Balanced and Readable say "shrine", a plainer word for the place of worship the term points to (m1).

source.text: לֹא־תָבִיא֩ אֶתְנַ֨ן זוֹנָ֜ה וּמְחִ֣יר כֶּ֗לֶב בֵּ֛ית יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ לְכָל־נֶ֑דֶר כִּ֧י תוֹעֲבַ֛ת יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ גַּם־שְׁנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Not you shall bring [the] hire of [a] prostitute and [the] price of [a] dog [into the] house of Yahweh your God for any vow, for [an] abomination of Yahweh your God [are] also both of them.

en.L: You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God for any vow, for both of them also [are] an abomination to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God.
en.B: Do not bring a prostitute's earnings or the wages of a male prostitute into the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God to pay any vow, because both are detestable to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God.
en.R: Do not bring money earned by a prostitute, woman or man, into the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God to pay for something you promised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God hates both kinds of payment.

decisions.choice: the price of a dog: the earnings of a male prostitute
alternatives: the price paid for a dog
decisions.reason: Set beside "the hire of a prostitute" and following the male cult prostitute of verse 18, "dog" here is most likely a scornful name for a male prostitute. Some take it literally, as money from the sale of a dog, an unclean animal.

decisions.choice: bring into the house of the LORD for any vow: pay a vow with such money
decisions.reason: A person who vowed to give God something paid it at the sanctuary (12:6, 11). Money earned in this way may not be given to the LORD, however it is offered.

decisions.choice: an abomination to the LORD, both of them: both kinds of payment are detestable to him
decisions.reason: "Abomination" names what the LORD finds utterly offensive (17:1). "Both of them" refers to the two payments named, the prostitute's hire and the dog's price.

decisions.choice: male prostitute / a prostitute, woman or man
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "dog". Balanced and Readable say who is meant (m1). Readable joins the two payments into one phrase.

decisions.choice: detestable / hates
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "abomination". Balanced says "detestable" and Readable says plainly that the LORD hates it, as in 17:1.

source.text: לֹא־תַשִּׁ֣יךְ לְאָחִ֔יךָ נֶ֥שֶׁךְ כֶּ֖סֶף נֶ֣שֶׁךְ אֹ֑כֶל נֶ֕שֶׁךְ כָּל־דָּבָ֖ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִשָּֽׁךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: Not you shall charge interest to your brother: interest of silver, interest of food, interest of any thing which is lent at interest.

en.L: You shall not charge interest to your brother: interest on silver, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent at interest.
en.B: Do not charge a fellow Israelite interest, whether on money, on food, or on anything else that can be lent for interest.
en.R: Do not make a fellow Israelite pay interest when you lend money, food or anything else.

decisions.choice: interest: any extra amount taken back on a loan
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "bite": what the lender takes beyond what he lent. Exodus 22:24 and Leviticus 25:35-37 forbid it on loans to a poor fellow Israelite. Loans in Israel were mostly help for those in need, not business.

decisions.choice: your brother: a fellow Israelite
decisions.reason: "Brother" means a member of the same people, as in 15:2-3, 7. Verse 21 sets him against the foreigner.

decisions.choice: silver: money
decisions.reason: Silver was weighed out as money, so "silver" means money (Genesis 23:16).

decisions.choice: a fellow Israelite ... money
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "your brother" and "silver". Balanced and Readable say what is meant (m2, m3).

source.text: לַנָּכְרִ֣י תַשִּׁ֔יךְ וּלְאָחִ֖יךָ לֹ֣א תַשִּׁ֑יךְ לְמַ֨עַן יְבָרֶכְךָ֜ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ בְּכֹל֙ מִשְׁלַ֣ח יָדֶ֔ךָ עַל־הָאָ֕רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֥ה בָא־שָׁ֖מָּה לְרִשְׁתָּֽהּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: To the foreigner you may charge interest, and to your brother not you shall charge interest, so that may bless you Yahweh your God in all [the] undertaking of your hand on the land which you [are] going there to possess it.

en.L: To the foreigner you may charge interest, but to your brother you shall not charge interest, so that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God may bless you in every undertaking of your hand in the land that you are going into to take possession of it.
en.B: You may charge interest to a foreigner, but not to a fellow Israelite, so that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God may bless you in everything you set your hand to in the land you are entering to take possession of.
en.R: You may charge interest to a foreigner, but not to a fellow Israelite. Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God will bless you in all your work in the land you are about to enter and make your own.

decisions.choice: the foreigner: an outsider, such as a trader from another land
decisions.reason: The word names a foreigner who is not part of Israel and not settled among them, unlike the sojourner who lives in Israel and is protected (10:18-19). A loan to such a person was usually a matter of trade, not help for the poor (15:3).

decisions.choice: so that the LORD your God may bless you: generosity to fellow Israelites brings God's blessing
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy often ties the LORD's blessing on all "the work of your hand" to kindness toward the needy (14:29; 15:10; 24:19). Giving up profit from a brother in need is not a loss, since the LORD gives the increase.

decisions.choice: everything you set your hand to
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "all the undertaking of your hand". Balanced keeps the picture of the hand; Readable says "all your work".

source.text: כִּֽי־תִדֹּ֥ר נֶ֨דֶר֙ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ לֹ֥א תְאַחֵ֖ר לְשַׁלְּמ֑וֹ כִּֽי־דָּרֹ֨שׁ יִדְרְשֶׁ֜נּוּ יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ מֵֽעִמָּ֔ךְ וְהָיָ֥ה בְךָ֖ חֵֽטְא׃

records.literal_gloss: When you vow [a] vow to Yahweh your God, not you shall delay to pay it, for surely will require it Yahweh your God from with you, and it will be in you sin.

en.L: When you vow a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, you shall not delay to pay it, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God will surely require it from you, and it will be sin in you.
en.B: When you make a vow to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, do not put off paying it, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God will certainly ask it of you, and you will be guilty of sin.
en.R: If you make a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, do not wait to keep it. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God will surely expect you to do what you promised. If you do not, you will be guilty of sin.

decisions.choice: vow a vow: a solemn promise to give God something
decisions.reason: A vow promised God a gift or an act, often if he answered a prayer (Genesis 28:20-22; Numbers 21:2; 1 Samuel 1:11). Numbers 30 sets out the rules on keeping vows. Ecclesiastes 5:3-4 repeats this warning.

decisions.choice: surely require: the verb is doubled for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Hebrew repeats the verb "require" to stress that God will certainly hold the one who vowed to his word.

decisions.choice: it will be sin in you: the unpaid vow counts as sin
decisions.reason: If the vow is not paid, the failure itself is a sin that rests on the one who made it.

decisions.choice: If you do not,
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the guilt comes from failing to keep the vow (m3).

decisions.choice: make a promise
decisions.reason: Readable says "promise" for "vow", as it does in verses 19 and 23-24.

source.text: וְכִ֥י תֶחְדַּ֖ל לִנְדֹּ֑ר לֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה בְךָ֖ חֵֽטְא׃

records.literal_gloss: And if you refrain from vowing, not it will be in you sin.

en.L: But if you refrain from vowing, it will not be sin in you.
en.B: But if you hold back from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin.
en.R: But if you choose not to make a promise, that is not a sin.

decisions.choice: vows are free: not making one is no sin
decisions.reason: No one is required to make a vow. The sin lies in promising and not keeping the promise (verse 22), so the safe path is not to vow at all rather than to vow carelessly (Ecclesiastes 5:4).

source.text: מוֹצָ֥א שְׂפָתֶ֖יךָ תִּשְׁמֹ֣ר וְעָשִׂ֑יתָ כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר נָדַ֜רְתָּ לַיהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ נְדָבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתָּ בְּפִֽיךָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: [The] utterance of your lips you shall keep and do, just as you vowed to Yahweh your God [a] freewill [gift], which you spoke with your mouth.

en.L: What goes out of your lips you shall keep and do, just as you vowed freely to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God what you spoke with your mouth.
en.B: Be careful to do what you have said, just as you freely vowed it to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God with your own mouth.
en.R: Be careful to do what you said you would do. You chose freely to make a promise to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, and you said it out loud yourself.

decisions.choice: freely: the vow was made by free choice
alternatives: you vowed a freewill offering to the LORD your God
decisions.reason: The word is the one for a freewill offering (12:6, 17). Here it most likely describes how the vow was made: of the person's own free will, which is why it binds him. It may instead name what was vowed, a freewill offering.

decisions.choice: what goes out of your lips ... what you spoke with your mouth: your own spoken words
decisions.reason: Both phrases stress that the vow was the person's own words, spoken aloud. Numbers 30:3 uses the same language: a man must do all that goes out of his mouth.

decisions.choice: what you have said / what you said you would do
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "what goes out of your lips". Balanced and Readable say it more plainly (m2).

source.text: כִּ֤י תָבֹא֙ בְּכֶ֣רֶם רֵעֶ֔ךָ וְאָכַלְתָּ֧ עֲנָבִ֛ים כְּנַפְשְׁךָ֖ שָׂבְעֶ֑ךָ וְאֶֽל־כֶּלְיְךָ֖ לֹ֥א תִתֵּֽן׃ס

records.literal_gloss: When you go into [the] vineyard of your neighbor, and you may eat grapes according to your appetite, your fill, but into your vessel not you shall put [any].

en.L: When you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat grapes as you desire, your fill, but you shall not put [any] into your container.
en.B: When you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat as many grapes as you like, until you are full, but do not put any into a basket.
en.R: When you walk through your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat all the grapes you want. But do not put any in a basket to take away.

decisions.choice: according to your appetite, your fill: as much as you want to eat
decisions.reason: The word often translated "soul" here means desire or appetite, and "your fill" means until you are satisfied. The person may eat freely on the spot.

decisions.choice: eat, but do not carry away: the hungry may eat, but not harvest
decisions.reason: The law lets anyone passing through a neighbor's vineyard satisfy hunger, while protecting the owner's crop from being gathered by others. It is one of several laws that make room for the needy in the harvest (24:19-21).

decisions.choice: a basket
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word means any container or vessel. Balanced and Readable say "basket", the usual container for carrying grapes; Literal says "container".

decisions.choice: to take away
decisions.reason: Readable states the point of the rule: the grapes may not be carried off (m2).

source.text: כִּ֤י תָבֹא֙ בְּקָמַ֣ת רֵעֶ֔ךָ וְקָטַפְתָּ֥ מְלִילֹ֖ת בְּיָדֶ֑ךָ וְחֶרְמֵשׁ֙ לֹ֣א תָנִ֔יף עַ֖ל קָמַ֥ת רֵעֶֽךָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: When you go into [the] standing grain of your neighbor, and you may pluck ears with your hand, but [a] sickle not you shall wield over [the] standing grain of your neighbor.

en.L: When you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck ears with your hand, but you shall not wield a sickle over your neighbor's standing grain.
en.B: When you go into your neighbor's field of standing grain, you may pick heads of grain with your hand, but do not take a sickle to your neighbor's grain.
en.R: When you walk through your neighbor's grain field, you may pick some grain with your hand. But do not cut any of your neighbor's grain with a sickle.

decisions.choice: pluck ears with your hand: pick a few heads of grain to eat on the spot
decisions.reason: As with the grapes in verse 25, someone passing may pick heads of ripe grain by hand and eat them, but may not reap with a sickle, which would be taking the harvest. Jesus' disciples did this on a Sabbath (Matthew 12:1; Mark 2:23; Luke 6:1); the question raised there was the day, not the picking.

decisions.choice: wield a sickle: put a sickle to the grain to reap it
decisions.reason: The verb means to swing or wave; with a sickle it means to cut the grain as a reaper does.

decisions.choice: heads of grain / some grain
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "ears". Balanced says "heads of grain", the usual modern term, and Readable says "some grain".
